source: Sabuncu, Boyer, High (2026) BCSER: Capacity Building for Developing a Troubleshooting Learning Environment (ASEE, paper 52353)
finding: Interviews with 18 senior engineers gave four kinds of complexity in troubleshooting: system representation, information ambiguity, situational, and stakeholder. Experts use prior schemas to choose knowledge types and reasoning strategies. The paper then defines five 'manifolds' (system dynamics, epistemic, normative, divergence, situational/stakeholder). Complexity is a mismatch between two or more manifolds that blocks progress.
numbers: 18 engineers, over 10 years each: 14 industry, 4 academic. 17 male, 1 female. 10 PhD, 2 MS, 6 BS. Think-aloud: 6 people run, 2 shown (one expert, one PhD student). No statistics.
quote: complexity arises when there is misalignment across layers such that movement toward resolution is blocked or destabilized
limits: Preliminary, qualitative, NSF grant 2422510, small sample, one female. Poster slides by the same author give 22 interviews and 6 think-alouds, so counts differ between sources. No LLM content.
agent_relevance: Gives a trigger list for operators: when the agent cannot tell if the system is even faulty (divergence vs situational mismatch), it should ask or verify, not search. Complexity types can label why a run stalls.

source: Sabuncu et al. (2026) same paper, think-aloud case: pneumatic compressor, two solvers (JOEY expert, HAZEL PhD student)
finding: On one ill-structured compressor fault case the expert sought system understanding first and sketched diagrams. The student sought system understanding only when it helped the root-cause search and drew nothing. The expert was unsure about system expertise; the student was unsure about incoherent cues in the problem.
numbers: N=2 shown of 6 run. Symptom: compressor shuts down after about 2 min, motor housing hot, tank pressure 20 to 25 psi below cut-out.
limits: Two cases only. No inference possible. The expert/student contrast is confounded with sketching habit.
agent_relevance: Two distinct opening moves: model-first or cause-first. Our scaffold could run both and compare, as separate samples, instead of fixing one.

source: Sabuncu et al. (2026) interview subgroup counts
finding: Engineers in defense, biomedical and product design reported more situational awareness. Biomedical and product design reported more ambiguity. PhD holders reported less collaborative problem solving than BS and MS holders. Troubleshooting is described as non-linear, non-sequential, recursive.
numbers: Group sizes given in text: defense n=4, biomedical n=8, product design n=13 (groups overlap, so they exceed 18).
limits: Text says data are too small for statistics. Counts of code mentions, not effects.
agent_relevance: Supports a loop with return edges (re-open earlier states) rather than a straight pipeline.

source: Daly, Anand, Abel, Sabuncu (2024) Industry Perspectives on Mechanical Engineering Troubleshooting (ASEE)
finding: Nine industry engineers described three phases: understand the problem, diagnostic techniques, resource management. Diagnostics were top-down, systematic ('peeling an onion'), pattern recognition from experience, adaptability and efficiency. A teaching framework lists 7 phases from identification to carrying out the fix.
numbers: 9 interviewees, 30 to 60 minutes each. Diagnostic-techniques theme appeared 22 times.
limits: N=9, self-report, no behaviour measured. Authors note interviewees did not cover all methods.
agent_relevance: Seven-phase list (identify, comprehend, collect data, hypothesis test, system analysis, find failure mode, fix) maps onto a state machine. 'Collect normal-operation reference data first' is a cheap first operator.

source: Tseng, Bogahawatta, Ginige, Patel, Dakic, Seneviratne (2026) FaulT-Bench: network troubleshooting LLM agents under unreliable user tickets
finding: With a real fault and an accurate ticket, three agents are near ceiling. Misleading tickets (wrong device, wrong cause) barely hurt. On healthy networks with a false fault report, agents keep probing until a harmless condition is promoted to a root cause, instead of saying nothing is wrong.
numbers: 200 scenarios, 8 topologies: 80 correct-fault, 72 false-premise, 24 wrong-device, 24 wrong-cause. Outcome score: correct-fault .932, wrong-device .957, wrong-cause .911, false-premise .820. 3 passes, 1,800 core runs. Over-diagnosis on healthy nets: SADE 24% (51/210), ReAct 16% (33/209), Claude Code 11% (21/198).
quote: they fail by continuing to probe until some genuine but benign standing network condition can be presented as the root cause
limits: Tickets are authored, not real helpdesk tickets. LLM judge. Three agents, one turn budget. ReAct runs on a different base model than Claude Code.
agent_relevance: Direct match for our stop rule. The agent needs an explicit 'no fault found' exit with evidence, and a guard against calling a benign oddity the cause (G-style anti-overclaim).

source: Tseng et al. (2026) FaulT-Bench persona experiment (E2): same 72 healthy networks, five ticket wordings
finding: How a ticket is written matters more than what it claims. A confident wrong ticket is handled like an accurate one, because the agent can test and refute a definite claim. A vague ticket leaves nothing to refute and degrades results. Removing certainty cost 0.182 outcome; removing identifiers cost a further 0.141. Added confidence to a vague ticket helped only +0.039. This is the reverse of the sycophancy expectation.
numbers: Outcome: Standard .820, Naive .820, Novice .675, Novice-confident .714, Naive-unsure .638, Naive-no-detail .497. Over-diagnosis 17%, 16%, 31%, 28%, 35%, 47%. Claude Code outcome fell from .870 (standard) to .283 (no detail) and 49% of its runs hit the turn limit; over-diagnosis for CC rose from 7% to 51% under Naive-unsure. Two passes per persona.
limits: Persona rewrites by the authors; one factor changed at a time but small cells (72). Differences of a few points not tested for significance.
agent_relevance: Trigger for an operator: if the input has no checkable identifiers, first convert it into testable claims (ask, or probe to get identifiers) before hypothesising.

source: Tseng et al. (2026) FaulT-Bench: failure styles and cost
finding: The three agents fail differently. SADE (skill playbooks) has the best grounded reasoning but a constant 20 to 34% false-alarm rate. Claude Code is best on the standard ticket but collapses under vague wording by returning no verdict. ReAct always answers but with the least grounded reasoning (reasoning .798 to .868). Effort follows the ticket, not the fault.
numbers: Tool calls per answered run 13 to 18 on real faults; Claude Code makes 30 on the no-detail rewrite vs 13, and reads 549k vs 136k tokens. Timeouts: 366 of 3,960 runs (9%) used 23% of US$1,525 total spend. Share of budget on no-answer runs: Claude Code 36%, SADE 10%, ReAct 14%. Skill playbooks gave SADE the worst over-diagnosis (24%).
limits: Three agents, different base models in one case, so cause of each style is not isolated.
agent_relevance: Playbooks (more ways to find something) can raise false positives. Budget rule: stop after N probes without new discriminating evidence.

source: NIKA authors (2025) NIKA: A Network Arena for Benchmarking AI Agents on Network Troubleshooting
finding: Larger models detect network faults much more reliably than they localise or explain them. Even the best model stays far from perfect. On indirect-symptom faults (resource contention) the agent stops at shallow, connectivity-centric explanations like 'link unstable' without linking CRC errors or queue drops to a deeper cause.
numbers: Detection / localisation / RCA accuracy: GPT-OSS:20B 19.0 / 5.5 / 5.5 %; GPT-5-mini 74.0 / 36.0 / 22.0 %; GPT-5 89.0 / 68.7 / 55.3 % (row order reconstructed from garbled table; text says GPT-5 beats mini by about 20% on detection, nearly 2x on localisation, over 2.5x on RCA). GPT-5 link failure localisation 97%, resource contention 58%. 54 issue types, 5 scenarios; more than 900 reasoning traces released.
limits: Emulated networks, three models, one run each assumed. Table text partly scrambled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Stopping at the first plausible explanation is the failure to design against: add a step 'does this cause explain every symptom, including the small ones?'.

source: NIKA authors (2025) NIKA: topology size and tool-use analysis
finding: Detection stays stable as the network grows, but localisation and root-cause accuracy fall. Token use nearly doubles. GPT-5 uses more tools but fewer reasoning steps than GPT-5-mini and writes more reasoning tokens. In failed runs GPT-5-mini made little use of higher-layer tools.
numbers: Networks of 11, 27 and 101 nodes on average (small, medium, large), four scenario families. GPT-5 input 105k vs GPT-5-mini 156k tokens; output 14.6k vs 6.5k; reasoning 12.3k vs 4.5k; runtime up about 50% for GPT-5.
limits: Four scenarios for the size test. Causal reading of tool use is by the authors.
agent_relevance: Complexity of the system (size, coupling) breaks localisation first. Operator trigger: when system is large, narrow with a hierarchy (half-split by subsystem) before deep probing.

source: Clark et al. (2026) SREGym: A Live Benchmark for AI SRE Agents with High-Fidelity Failure Scenarios
finding: On 90 live cloud failure problems, frontier agents solve diagnosis 38 to 73% of the time. Added ambient noise (distracting faults) lowers diagnosis for every agent-model pair, because agents take the first plausible anomaly as the target failure and then ignore real evidence once found.
numbers: Diagnosis / mitigation / end-to-end: Stratus+Sonnet-4.6 61.5 / 78.5 / 54.8 %; Claude Code+Sonnet-4.6 72.6 / 75.6 / 60.7 %; Codex+GPT-5.4 70.0 / 63.7 / 53.3 %; Stratus+Kimi K2.5 40.4 / 40.4 / 27.4 %. With noise (second row of each pair, inferred from text): Claude Code diagnosis 62.6%, Codex 59.3%, Stratus+Sonnet 51.5%, Stratus+K2.5 38.1%. 3 runs per problem.
limits: Which table row is noise vs no-noise is inferred from the text. Grading by an LLM oracle (kappa .90 against humans).
agent_relevance: Concrete anchoring failure with numbers. Operator: keep 2 or more live hypotheses; require evidence that rules out the distractor before locking in.

source: Clark et al. (2026) SREGym: new failure scenarios vs ported ones
finding: Agents do well on problems ported from older benchmarks but drop sharply on new, harder failure types (metastable, correlated failures). Complexity of the fault, not the tooling, drives the drop.
numbers: End-to-end success on ported (n=34) vs new failures (n=13): Stratus+Sonnet-4.6 63.7% to 17.9%; Claude Code 60.8% to 28.2%; Codex 57.8% to 15.4%. Ported-problem diagnosis for Stratus 70.6% vs 33.3% on new. Also: 44% of mitigation problems in older sets can be solved by a generic pod-restart loop.
limits: Only 13 new-failure problems. Old benchmarks partly contaminated by easy cases.
agent_relevance: Warns that results on simple benchmarks hide failure on coupled, delayed, nonlinear systems (the 'system dynamics manifold' of c01).

source: Kim, Park, Yun, Lee (2026) Why Do AI Agents Systematically Fail at Cloud Root Cause Analysis?
finding: Process-level analysis of 1,675 OpenRCA agent runs found 12 failure types. Most common: hallucinated reading of data and incomplete exploration, across all five models. Symptom-as-cause and no cross-validation also appear. Authors argue failures come from the shared agent framework, not model strength.
numbers: Baseline OpenRCA agent perfect accuracy 3.9% (Claude Sonnet 4) to 12.5% (Gemini 2.5 Pro); GPT-5 mini 8.4, GPT-OSS 120B 6.9, Solar Pro 2 5.7. Pitfall rates over runs: hallucinated interpretation 71.2%, incomplete exploration 63.9%, symptom-as-cause 39.9%, code error 27.2%, timestamp error 23.3%, no cross-validation 18.6%, instruction-code mismatch 18.8%, meaningless repetition 8.3%, misattributed evidence 3.4%.
limits: Pitfalls are counted per run and can co-occur, so they sum above 100%. Labelling pipeline is LLM-assisted. OpenRCA's own strict scoring.
agent_relevance: A ready checklist of failure modes for a verifier step: symptom-as-cause, no cross-check, skipped components.

source: Kim et al. (2026) mitigation experiments
finding: Prompt-level fixes did not help. Hypothesis-driven prompting widened exploration (new hypotheses like memory utilisation appeared) but the model still invented readings of the data. Pitfall-aware prompting: the model quoted the pitfall list in its reasoning and repeated the same errors. Enriching what agents pass each other (code, raw errors) cut communication failures by up to 15 points.
numbers: Test on Claude Sonnet 4, 70 Bank-domain tasks. Enriched protocol: perfect detections GPT-5 mini 0 to 2 (0.0 to 4.9%), Gemini 2.5 Pro 1 to 3 (2.4 to 7.3%), Solar Pro 2 2 to 3. Steps per run -22.1% (11.9 to 9.2), tokens per step +24.8%, total tokens -1.6%, time -22.3%.
limits: Tiny absolute counts (0 to 3 of 41 tasks). Only one change per category tested. Gains on accuracy are within noise at this size.
agent_relevance: Strong caution: telling the model about biases or asking for hypotheses is not enough. Put checks in code or structure (external verification of claims), consistent with our guardrails.

source: OpenRCA authors (2025) OpenRCA: Can LLMs Locate the Root Cause of Software Failures? (ICLR 2025)
finding: Benchmark of 335 failures from 3 enterprise systems with over 68 GB of telemetry. Best result with the RCA-agent was Claude 3.5 Sonnet at 11.34% solved. Scoring needs all root-cause elements right.
numbers: Per search-result summary: Claude 3.5 + RCA-agent 11.34% correct, 17.31% partial; GPT-4o + RCA-agent 8.96% / 17.91%; Gemini 1.5 Pro prompting 7.16% / 23.58%.
limits: I did not open the paper. Numbers are from a search summary of the project page, not read in full. Page and OpenReview fetches returned nothing usable. The pitfall paper (c12) lists Claude Sonnet 3.5 at 11.3 overall, matching.
agent_relevance: Shows the low ceiling on realistic multi-source diagnosis as of 2024 to 2025.

source: AIOpsLab authors (2025) AIOpsLab: A Holistic Framework to Evaluate AI Agents for Enabling Autonomous Clouds
finding: 48 problems across detection, localisation, analysis and mitigation. Detection (binary) was not solved by most agents. Analysis and mitigation were hardest. All LLM agents beat classic non-LLM detection and localisation methods. More steps help ReAct and FLASH, but GPT-3.5 stops improving after about 5 steps.
numbers: Overall accuracy: FLASH 59.32% (best at step limit 20), ReAct 55.93%, GPT-4 with shell 49.15%, GPT-3.5 with shell 15.25%. Only FLASH answered all detection problems correctly. ReAct best at top-3 localisation but worse at top-1. GPT-3.5 shell agent recovered no failure in mitigation.
limits: Row labels reconstructed from a scrambled table and checked against text (GPT-3.5 lowest at 15.25%, FLASH highest). One application set mainly.
agent_relevance: Self-repair from environment feedback saturates quickly in diagnosis, unlike code tasks with tests. Needs planning and an explicit discriminating step.

source: ITBench authors (2025) ITBench: Evaluating AI Agents across Diverse Real-World IT Automation Tasks
finding: On 94 real-world scenarios the best agents with state-of-the-art models resolved few: SRE incidents, security compliance, and cost operations.
numbers: 13.8% of SRE scenarios, 25.2% of CISO scenarios, 0% of FinOps scenarios. 94 scenarios in total.
limits: Only the abstract and introduction were read, not the results sections. Breakdown by model not recorded.
agent_relevance: A hard baseline: realistic incident resolution is far from solved in 2025.

source: RCAgent authors (2024) RCAgent: Cloud Root Cause Analysis by Autonomous Agents with Tool-Augmented LLMs (CIKM 2024)
finding: A tool-using agent with self-consistency over action trajectories, context management and domain knowledge beat plain ReAct on root cause, solution, evidence and responsibility prediction for Alibaba Flink jobs. It is deployed in a production diagnosis workflow.
numbers: G-Correctness (LLM judge, 0 to 10) ReAct 3.06 vs RCAgent 5.22; METEOR 6.44 vs 15.15. Stability: pass rate 99.38% within 15 steps, invalid action rate 7.93%. Removing a JSON-repair tool dropped pass rate by 33.54% (70.95% invalid rate). Without several parts it fell to 70.19% pass rate and 44.80% invalid.
limits: Internal model, one company, 15,616 anomalous jobs from one month, judge is an LLM with human check. Several ablation labels were lost in extraction.
agent_relevance: Sampling several independent investigation trajectories and aggregating (like our many-attempts state) works in diagnosis, even though plain ReAct lags.

source: Pei et al. (2025) Flow-of-Action: SOP Enhanced LLM-Based Multi-Agent System for Root Cause Analysis (WWW Companion 2025)
finding: Encoding human SRE diagnosis procedures (SOPs) as retrievable knowledge plus a tool that turns them into code lifted accuracy sharply over ReAct, Reflexion and CoT. Removing the SOP knowledge dropped location accuracy from 54% to 8.6% on GPT-3.5.
numbers: Average of location (LA) and type (TA) accuracy: Flow-of-Action with GPT-4-Turbo 64.01 (LA 70.89, TA 57.12) vs ReAct GPT-4-Turbo 35.50, Reflexion GPT-3.5 54.06, CoT GPT-4-Turbo 32.61, K8sGPT/HolmesGPT 11.11. Ablation (GPT-3.5): full 54.06; without SOP knowledge 15.39; without SOP flow 27.50; without action set 42.34; judge/observation/action agents removed about 33.7 to 35.0.
limits: Authors' own benchmark of injected Kubernetes faults (CPU/memory stress and others); ByteDance. No independent replication. Reflexion with GPT-3.5 beats ReAct with GPT-4-Turbo on the average, which shows scatter by backbone.
agent_relevance: The closest published use of expert procedure inside an LLM agent loop: expert steps as constraints at 'crucial junctures'. Supports state-machine scaffolds from expert troubleshooting models.

source: Ahmed, Ghosh, Bansal, Zimmermann, Zhang, Rajmohan (2023) Recommending Root-Cause and Mitigation Steps for Cloud Incidents using LLMs (ICSE 2023)
finding: First large study of GPT-3.x for incident root causes and mitigations on Microsoft incidents. Fine-tuned models beat zero-shot. Multi-task training did not beat single-task. Machine-detected incidents were easier than human-detected ones. Incident owners judged outputs useful.
numbers: More than 40,000 incidents. Code-davinci-002 gain over Davinci 23.26% (BLEU-4 top1) and 42.16% on METEOR-type metric for root cause. Multi-task: Curie and Codex fell by 2.8% BLEU-4, 2.0% ROUGE-L, 7.2% Meteor; mitigation down 4.1% on average. Machine-detected beat human-detected by 9.5% BLEU-4, 20% ROUGE-L, 23% METEOR. Human rating: mean correctness and readability 3.52 to 4.64 of 5; more than 70% of owners rated 3 or above.
limits: Text-similarity metrics poorly match correctness (authors say so). Human panel size not recorded here. Old GPT-3 era models.
agent_relevance: Models were used as suggesters from past incident text, not as investigators. Past cases help; this is the memory side of troubleshooting.

source: Cai et al. (2026) A Multi-Dataset Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agents in Microservice Failure Diagnosis (AIOps2025 and RCA100)
finding: Existing benchmarks grade only the final answer. This one scores three things: where the fault is, what type it is, and whether the reasoning trace is grounded in evidence (labelled causal chains and evidence checkpoints). Most cases need more than one data type.
numbers: Over 500 expert-labelled cases from two systems; 400 HipsterShop cases in AIOps2025: 62.5% need 2 or more data types, 31% need all three (metrics, logs, traces); metric evidence needed in 92.8%, log 56.2%, trace 43.0%. RCA100: 103 cases, 92.2% of chains cross 2 or more entity types, 19.4% cross APM to Kubernetes. Competition with over 6,000 teams.
limits: The paper is dataset-focused; I found no model score table in it. Agent results not recorded.
agent_relevance: Gives a grading idea: score evidence-grounded reasoning, not only the answer. Useful for judging our scaffold's traces.

source: Wu et al. (2025) TN-AutoRCA: Benchmark Construction and Agentic Framework for Self-Improving Alarm-Based Root Cause Analysis in Telecom Networks
finding: 530 telecom fault scenarios built from expert knowledge graphs. Top LLMs reach F1 below 70% when asked directly. An evaluate-analyse-repair loop on generated solution code, driven by contrastive feedback across all failure cases, raised F1 from 58.99% to 91.79%.
numbers: 530 scenarios, 94.5% classified 'Difficult'. Gemini-2.5-Pro direct F1 58.99%; best baseline F1@1 0.6254 (Qwen3-235B on mixed scenarios); Auto-RCA 91.79%.
limits: Task is graph path search over alarms, so it is closer to model-based diagnosis than to human troubleshooting. Test set also used to drive the repair loop, so generalisation is unclear (I did not check the split).
agent_relevance: Relevant: letting the model write a program that reasons over the system graph, and repairing it from patterns across failures, beats asking the model to reason directly.

source: Zhang, Li, Tian, Bachras, Jacobsen (2026) When Agentic Executions Fail: Detecting and Localizing Runtime Faults from Telemetry (AgentChaosBench)
finding: Diagnosing faults in LLM agent systems themselves from their traces is hard for zero-shot LLMs. Bypassed guardrails are almost unsolved from a single trace. An aligned no-fault reference helps some relative faults only.
numbers: 275 traces (250 faulty plus 25 no-fault control), 5 applications, 10 fault types. Fault-type top-1: DeepSeek-v4-pro 24.8% (top-3 34.0%), Qwen3.5-9B 19.2%; random about 9%. Component location top-1 at most 31%; type plus location jointly at most 22%. Compact structured view vs raw trace: 21.6/36.0 raw vs 24.8/34.0 structured for the best model.
limits: Zero-shot baselines only. Small local Qwen models lose runs to truncation (up to 33% for Qwen3.5-9B).
agent_relevance: Troubleshooting the agent itself is a use case: an agent that self-debugs from its own trace should expect low accuracy and need a reference run.

source: Hu and Ash (2026) LLM help with circuit debugging (as summarised in SUBFIELDS.md of this project)
finding: Per this project's earlier note: LLMs gave sensible suggestions for circuit debugging but struggled with images and sounded overconfident.
numbers: None recorded in the note.
limits: I could not open this paper: search budget used and API rate limits. No URL confirmed; the url above is a search page, not the paper.
agent_relevance: Overconfident tone matches the guardrail against unsupported certainty; image-reading failures mean the agent should ask for text readings of meters and scopes.

source: Tseng et al. (2026) FaulT-Bench: what accurate-ticket evaluation hides
finding: As long as a real fault exists, an agent that verifies the ticket and one that blindly follows it reach the same diagnosis, so the two cannot be told apart. They separate only on false reports. The authors call treating the ticket as a hypothesis, not an instruction, a skill distinct from diagnostic skill.
numbers: Wrong-device ticket shifts accuracy +2.5 points and wrong-cause -2.1 points versus the correct-fault mean (.932). Ticket phrasing alone changes accuracy by up to 14.5 points. 8% of (scenario, agent) cells move 0.5 or more between passes.
limits: Run noise is high; they report three-pass means. Authored tickets.
agent_relevance: Test our scaffold on cases where the premise is false. Absence-of-fault is the discriminating test of verification.

source: Kim et al. (2026) cross-check of agent step-use and exploration
finding: Agents narrow scope early: they skip relevant KPIs and components (incomplete exploration) and accept the first anomaly as the root cause (symptom-as-cause). Model strength changes code errors a lot but not these two.
numbers: Code generation error ranges from 1.8% (Gemini 2.5 Pro) to 65.5% (Claude Sonnet 4); symptom-as-cause peaks above 45% for GPT-5 mini and GPT-OSS 120B (up to 68.4% in one cell); hallucinated interpretation stays above 66% and incomplete exploration above 53% for every model.
limits: Per-model cells have a few hundred runs each. Percent cells could not all be matched to model columns because of table layout.
agent_relevance: Two failure types that no model fixes: both can be checked by a verifier asking 'what did we not look at, and does the cause explain the earlier symptom?'

source: Daly et al. (2024) interviews: how experts start and who they talk to
finding: Experts first define the problem with customers and stakeholders, gather manuals and field data for normal behaviour, use past incident archives ('troubleshooting problems are rarely unique'), and use visual maps (flow charts, logic paths). One life-critical case was solved by remote field data that showed a voltage spike unique to the affected device. Interviewees described two types of novice: those who ask for help immediately and those who do not.
numbers: N=9; no counts besides theme frequency (22 instances for diagnostics).
limits: Anecdote-level, no behavioural measure.
agent_relevance: Operators: get a normal-behaviour baseline; retrieve similar past cases; draw the system as a diagram before hypothesising.

source: Clark et al. (2026) SREGym: grading and noise mechanisms
finding: Diagnosis grading by an LLM oracle agrees with humans (Cohen kappa 0.90) and other LLM judges closely. Mitigation holds up better than diagnosis under noise because agents recover with greedy restarts. In some runs the agent had seen root-cause evidence but dismissed it as irrelevant to the (wrong) target.
numbers: Oracle kappa 0.90 vs human. Agreement between graders 0.76 to 0.97 in the table. Three runs per problem per agent-model pair.
limits: Judge is an LLM (Sonnet-4.6) which is also one of the tested models.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence rule: when new evidence contradicts the working target, the loop must re-open the hypothesis set instead of explaining the evidence away.
